name: Sharla Boehm
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. UCLA mathematics degree and teaching credential around 1951 (age ~21–22) are ordinary education; pioneering packet-switching simulation work with Paul Baran at RAND began around 1959–1960 (age ~30) and the key 1964 distributed-communications paper was at age ~34.
early_history_summary: Born in Seattle in 1929, raised in Santa Monica by a single mother who immigrated from Sweden. Studied mathematics at UCLA (class of 1951), taught math in public schools and for the U.S. Navy in London, then joined RAND Corporation in 1959 where she programmed early packet-switching simulations.
family_context_summary: Raised in Santa Monica during the Depression by a single mother from Sweden after family upheaval; limited household means.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented as a computing or technical-domain family background.
evidence_summary: Sharla Boehm’s historically important contribution was programming packet-switching / hot-potato routing simulations with Paul Baran at RAND in the early 1960s, well after age 26. Reviewed sources do not document a dated, material technical milestone at or before age 26.

name: Selmer Bringsjord
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. BA in philosophy from Penn and PhD from Brown (The Failure of Computationalism, 1987) completed at age ~28–29; first technical book What Robots Can and Can't Be (1992) and novel Soft Wars (1991) came in his early 30s.
early_history_summary: Born November 24, 1958. Studied philosophy at the University of Pennsylvania and completed a PhD under Roderick Chisholm at Brown in 1987. Later became professor of computer science and cognitive science at RPI and director of the RAIR Lab.
evidence_summary: Bringsjord’s documented career milestones (PhD 1987, first books early 1990s, long RPI faculty career in logic-based AI) all fall after age 26. No independently verified material breakout by age 26 was found.

name: Rob Sanheim

BS in Management Computer Systems from UW Whitewater in 2001; early career at Brown Shoe and consulting; notable GitHub senior engineer work (Protected Branches, PR Reviews) was 2012–2017, years after any plausible age-26 window.
early_history_summary: Software engineer with 20+ years experience. Employee #5 at Relevance/Cognitect, later senior engineer at GitHub (2012–2017), then roles at Bold Penguin, Simple.org, Monograph, and Doximity. No public Wikipedia page or documented birth year.
evidence_summary: Without a confirmed birth year, age at early career steps cannot be verified. Public resume milestones that would count as material (GitHub senior engineering, Cognitect principal) are mid-career rather than age-26 breakouts.

name: Nathaniel Borenstein
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. BA Grinnell 1980 (age ~22–23) and CMU PhD in 1985 (age ~27–28); Andrew Message System work was during graduate school; MIME standards work and first MIME email attachment (1992) and First Virtual (1994) all came well after 26.
early_history_summary: Born September 23, 1957. Attended Ohio State, Deep Springs, Hebrew University, then Grinnell (BA 1980) and Carnegie Mellon (PhD CS 1985). Later designed MIME at Bellcore, founded First Virtual Holdings, and became Mimecast chief scientist.
family_context_summary: Described as from a conservative middle-class Jewish family; three brothers include academic Eliot Borenstein and journalist Seth Borenstein. Early child academic acceleration noted in personal essays.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented as a computing-domain family advantage.
evidence_summary: Borenstein’s defining contribution (MIME co-design and first email attachment) occurred in the early 1990s when he was in his mid-30s. Graduate work on Andrew Message System does not yield a clearly dated material external milestone by age 26.

name: Olivier Chapelle
milestone_by_age_26: Published the highly cited Machine Learning journal paper “Choosing Multiple Parameters for Support Vector Machines” (with Vapnik, Bousquet, and Mukherjee; ~2002, age ~24) and earlier NIPS 2000 work on Vicinal Risk Minimization; defended PhD on SVMs at Université Pierre et Marie Curie / LIP6 in 2004 (age ~26).
early_history_summary: French machine learning researcher who interned in Yann LeCun’s AT&T lab around 1998, worked with Vladimir Vapnik and colleagues on SVM model selection, earned a PhD in 2004 under Patrick Gallinari, and became known for semi-supervised learning and industrial ML research (Yahoo Research; later Google).
primary_early_advantage_tags: SVM research, Vapnik, LeCun AT&T, LIP6 PhD, semi-supervised learning
evidence_summary: Chapelle entered frontier ML early via an AT&T research internship with LeCun’s group, then co-authored foundational SVM model-selection work with Vapnik while still in his mid-20s. His 2002 Machine Learning paper and 2000 NIPS contribution, followed by a 2004 PhD, establish a clear research breakout by age 26. Later he co-edited the influential Semi-Supervised Learning volume and worked as a senior industrial ML researcher; he died in 2020 at age 42.
starting_point: Not documented in reviewed sources beyond French academic training and early research internships; birth year inferred as ~1978 from NeurIPS memorial reporting death at age 42 in 2020.
current_position: Died in 2020 at age 42 after illness; remembered as a leading machine learning researcher of his generation (SVMs, semi-supervised learning), with senior industrial research roles including Yahoo Research and Google.

trajectory.event: Began research as an intern in Yann LeCun’s AT&T Labs group, working with Patrick Haffner and Vladimir Vapnik’s circle.
Published Vicinal Risk Minimization work at NIPS with Jason Weston and Léon Bottou.
Published “Choosing Multiple Parameters for Support Vector Machines” in Machine Learning with Vapnik, Bousquet, and Mukherjee—a highly cited model-selection contribution.
Defended PhD on SVMs (induction principles, automatic tuning, prior knowledge) at LIP6 / UPMC under Patrick Gallinari.
Co-edited the MIT Press volume Semi-Supervised Learning with Bernhard Schölkopf and Alexander Zien, a standard reference in the field.
Continued as a senior industrial ML researcher (Yahoo Research and later Google), applying large-scale learning methods.
Died after a severe illness; NeurIPS held a memorial recognizing him among the best ML researchers of his generation.

name: Andy Fang
milestone_by_age_26: Co-founded DoorDash (initially PaloAltoDelivery) in 2013 at age ~21 while a Stanford CS student with Tony Xu, Stanley Tang, and Evan Moore; served as founding CTO from May 2013, building the early delivery marketplace that later IPO’d.
early_history_summary: Born in San Jose in 1992 to Taiwanese immigrant parents, youngest of four. Attended The Harker School (class of 2010), then Stanford for CS. Learned basic coding in elementary school via a summer class his mother required; roomed with Stanley Tang and built side apps before the Startup Garage class that spawned DoorDash.
family_context_summary: Youngest of four children of Taiwanese immigrants in the San Jose / Bay Area; parents supportive of education and early coding exposure; attended elite private school Harker.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents not documented as tech operators; mother pushed summer coding class; immigrant middle/upper-middle professional path into Silicon Valley education pipeline.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Stanford, Harker, Silicon Valley, DoorDash cofounders, Startup Garage, on-demand delivery wave
evidence_summary: Fang’s age-21 DoorDash founding is independently documented (Wikipedia, Forbes, Harker alumni sources). Early advantages were geographic (Bay Area), institutional (Harker + Stanford Startup Garage), and peer-team (Xu, Tang, Moore), plus early coding exposure rather than inherited tech-domain capital. He was founding CTO, then scaled consumer engineering as DoorDash became the leading U.S. food-delivery platform and IPO’d in 2020.
starting_point: Born 1992 in San Jose to Taiwanese immigrant parents; youngest of four; raised near San Jose and educated at The Harker School before Stanford CS.
current_position: Co-founder and director of DoorDash; Head of LaunchPad / consumer engineering leadership roles; billionaire after 2020 IPO (Forbes net worth estimates ~$1.8B as of late 2025).

trajectory.event: Graduated from The Harker School and entered Stanford University to study computer science.
Co-founded DoorDash (from PaloAltoDelivery / Startup Garage) and became founding CTO, making early deliveries with cofounders.
Named with Stanley Tang to Forbes 30 Under 30 in Consumer Technology as DoorDash scaled nationally.
Transitioned from CTO (through Feb 2019) into broader product/engineering leadership as the company matured.
DoorDash IPO made Fang a billionaire co-founder as the company listed publicly.
Became Head of LaunchPad, DoorDash’s new software-products team, while remaining a board director.
Married Canadian tennis player and Stanford classmate Carol Zhao.

name: Bruce Bastian
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Mission, BYU music BA and CS master’s, and marching-band software with Alan Ashton were formative but company founding of WordPerfect / Satellite Software International occurred in 1978–1979 at age ~30–31.
early_history_summary: Born March 23, 1948 in Twin Falls, Idaho; raised LDS; missionary in Italy; BA Music and MS Computer Science at BYU; directed BYU Cougar Marching Band and built band-choreography software with Alan Ashton; later co-founded WordPerfect.
family_context_summary: Raised in Idaho in an LDS household; later came out as gay, divorced, and became a major LGBTQ+ philanthropist.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented as a software-industry family background.
evidence_summary: WordPerfect’s founding and PC-era success came when Bastian was about 30–34. No specific dated commercial or research breakout by age 26 is documented.

evidence_summary: Conservative reading treats PhD + new-faculty appointment as career-track steps rather than material public milestones; Abu-Mostafa’s field-shaping NeurIPS role and widely used ML course/book came later.
